I got really lucky, and I am eligible for a 5 week sabbatical starting anytime after August 2016. I know this is more than a year away, but I want to start some initial planning and saving now. I realize I may not be able to hit all of the things I mentioned below in one trip in this post, but I'd like to get some ideas.

I've never really left the east coast of the US. I've been to Vegas once and the Bahamas twice. I have my eye on Europe or Australia for my sabbatical. I'm 31 and I'm sad that I've never been outside of the US, I feel sheltered and want to take advantage of this 5 week long sabbatical.

Budget As most people will likely say, they want their trip to be as affordable as possible. I have $5k set aside already dedicated for traveling, and I'm hoping to save up at least another $2-3 specifically for traveling by next August. I'm looking to just factor in flights, hotel/hostel, and food.

Climate I hate really cold weather. Anything below 50F during the day is going to be way too cold for me. I love the water - rivers, lakes, oceans are great! I love to be on boats and swim. I also love historical downtown areas and beautiful country sides.

Wants I'd like to go to museums (art and science are my favorite), I want to experience good local food (I'm moderately adventurous), being able to swim in beautiful clear blue water would be a plus, I'd also like to experience the outdoors - I'm okay with camping. Since I've never traveled outside of the US (except for the bahamas, but that doesn't really count), I'm eager to see famous painting, famous monuments, famous historical sites or buildings, things that I've always see in books or on traveling shows aired on PBS. It sounds basic, but they are things I've never experienced first hand.

Other Most of my trip will be solo. My SO will only be able to take 1-2 weeks off to travel with me, and I want to spend the entire 5 weeks traveling abroad.

Safety I'll be alone most of my trip

I don't know what my best approach would be - stay in one part of the world for 5 weeks to see as much as possible? Or visit as many cities as possible over the course of 5 weeks? I'm narrowing down my options to the following-

Stay in 3-4 European countries (considering: France, UK, Spain, Italy, German or Czech Republic). I've wanted to go to Europe since I was a kid. I love French and German food. I've always loved learning about the Renaissance, art from Europe, I want to see Paris and the French country side, I want to drink beer in Prague, I want to eat all the food in Italy and Germany. I want to see castles and visit distilleries in Scotland. I want to visit areas of Ireland where they still speak Gaelic.

Participate in one of those 20-35 day multi-city tour of Europe - I'd be able to cover a lot! But, I'd only 1-3 days in each city.

Go to Australia and New Zealand - I feel like it's harder to travel to this area of the world if you're leaving from the US. It's going to be easier for me in the future to take 2 weeks off to go to Europe, than it would be to go to AUS. I also understand that you can get really cheap flights from one major city to another in AUS. I love the outdoors and the heat. For someone with little travel experience these places seem fairly exotic to me .
Where to go for 5 weeks? Europe or Australia? I have very little experience traveling abroad. I'm hoping to get some good feedback here!

I don´t know about NZ and AUS, and I haven´t done a lot of travel in Europe either, but as a german it seems to me that the stuff you wanna see (museums, monuments and historical buildings) sounds more like Europe than NZ/AUS. If you are going in August it should be warm almost everywhere, so that shouldn´t be a problem. The infrastructure in Europe is really good, getting around is fairly easy.

You don´t have to worry about your safety, the only problem you could encounter are petty thefts at big citys/tourist attractions, and even that is really unlikely.

The thing about Europe, and propably every other part of the world, is, there is a LOT to see. So my advice would be to only visit one or two countrys, maybe 3, so you have a little more time at each place to get to know your way around, get to know some people or visit the surrounding areas. Which countrys to visit depends on you. Eastern Europe is a little more laid back, there is more nature and it is not so crowded. In western Europe are a lot of people, big citys and a lot of things to do/see.

But in the end, it all depends on what you want to see, or where you want to go.

If you have any specific questions, don´t be shy, just PM me and I will answer you to the best of my knowledge.

For travelling in EU an InterRail-Ticket could be an interesting option for you. I travelled with the Ticket last year. I was a bit disappointed with what it offered to me (well more than a bit) because my parents travelled trough EU with InterRail years ago and they could take every train at every given time. That's not the case any more. That means you have to check which types of trains are included in the Ticket and you should look for a rod beforehand but since you have still a lot of time before you start your journey i guess it's not too bad. (I tried to plan the rod 1 week before i went). If you are planning to go by yourself and you want to meet people you should go to hostels. There are really good ones in EU. (My favourite one was in Porto: Gallery Hostel don't think it can get any better than this ;D )

I had basically your requirements and I decided to do Europe. I'm going in September for 3 weeks. I was going to do almost your trip but settled for Spain - Italy - Germany. I feel the same way about Italy as you do. That is the highlight of my trip, and the largest amount of time spent in that country.

With regards to the timing, I'd suggest you go either in spring or fall. I'd say lean more towards Fall, as that's what I'm doing and you get the tail end of the crazy busy tourist season and most monuments (that are perhaps being worked on/constructed on) will be open. The weather is most likely going to be around 20 degrees Celsius around that time.

Maybe you can fly in and out of UK, and take flights around from one place to another, or trains if you're visiting different cities in one country. (Italy is the easiest in this situation for trains). When I was planning my trip, I avoided expensive cities like Paris -- just staying there was super expensive, I found, so wasn't too too worried about getting it in our itinerary.

Tips:

  • budget for about 40-50 Euro per day for food, most people only eat two meals a day, and sometimes a really light lunch. 35*40=1400 euro.
  • budget for under 1000 for flight from american to europe. go to skyscanner.com and you'll get the cheapest flights. when I was looking I found one for ~400 USD, so you'd probably get a sick deal!
  • I don't know about you whether you're comfortable staying at a hostel, but use airbnb over hotels and start booking them about 6 months prior to your trip. make sure you're reading the reviews and not getting a shady place.
  • use ryanair or iberia for flights between countries. they're super cheap. however you do have to pay for luggage.
  • DO NOT BUY the rail pass, it's a rip off. (but the UK one is okay, I guess, Not too sure but don't get the eurorail pass!)

I know this got asked all the time on ... another website I used to frequent ... but about 40% of the time, it got a really good, creepy thread started that I always ended up reading just as I went to bed.

So, let's continue the tradition.

I've been "kidnapped" by "aliens", and seen what I can only call a ghost ... anybody else have any stories?
Is it too early to ask Voat to share their supernatural experiences?

Never too early to talk about the supernatural!

I'm not a big believer... I'd guess that 99.9% of what people think are supernatural experiences are probably just something else. I'm just a data/science type of person. However, that said, I can't help but say that maybe Shakespeare was right and that there are more things in Heaven and Earth than dreamped of in our philosophies.

For me, it was a fortune teller in Taiwan that my parents saw - most fortune tellers are obviously phony, they ask leading questions, try to sum you up, make vague predictions. Without asking any questions, this guy described people down to their very soul - the level of detail was just beyond any possible probability. He also predicted some important concrete future events down to the very day.

His story was pretty creepy too - he claims that he wasn't born with the ability, but as a tourist was in a sightseeing plane ride about the Grand Canyon when the plane crashed. As the plane was going down, he said that he felt something reach in and pull him out and when he awoke, he was in the wreckage and things went on somewhat normally until someone in his building (an old Korean man) stopped him and told him that he was different than other people, and brought him into his home to look at some of the fortune telling books that he had. Since then, he claims to have the ability to see things, including ghosts who roam our world.

It's interesting, but either way, I don't think that it's something you should live your every day life around - the real world is already surreal and adventure filled enough.

PS - however, I do believe that Stephen King may have some paranormal ability to be able to see into these other worlds... I read an interview response from him once where he cryptically said that he would never see a psychic or medium because we are so close to that world already as it is...

I'm 'psychic' and predict the deaths of people related to me in some way. Don't always know who it is, or how it's going to happen. I had my grandfather's death down to the day and was able to forewarn my aunt who was power of attorney so she could start getting prepared.

Best proof I can give, believe it or not, s'up to you.
